It initiates the preparation of Panchayat Development Plans for the financial year 2027–28 through citizen participation and evidence-based planning.
Special Gram Sabhas brought rural residents, elected representatives, Panchayat functionaries and officials together to review schemes and identify local priorities.
More than 2.42 lakh Special Gram Sabhas were scheduled on the GPDP and Panchayat NIRNAY portals.
PPC, also known as Jan Yojana Abhiyan, was first launched on 2 October 2018. It is an annual exercise to strengthen participatory, transparent and accountable rural governance.

Gram Panchayats prepare Gram Panchayat Development Plans (GPDPs), Block Panchayats prepare Block Panchayat Development Plans (BPDPs) and District Panchayats prepare District Panchayat Development Plans (DPDPs). Block and district plans support coordination, convergence and the scaling of local initiatives.
Village Prosperity and Resilience Plans (VPRPs), prepared by SHG federations, bring community priorities into Panchayat plans.
More than 2.55 lakh Gram Panchayats prepare participatory GPDPs and upload them on eGramSwaraj.
As of 29 July 2025, more than 18.13 lakh Panchayat Development Plans had been uploaded for 2019–20 to 2025–26: over 17.73 lakh GPDPs, 35,755 BPDPs and 3,469 DPDPs.

articles.title: The Public Examinations Prevention of Unfair Means Amendment Act 2026

runs: The Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Act, 2026, amends the 2024 Act, which came into force on June 21, 2024.
Dr. Jitendra Singh introduced the Bill in the Lok Sabha on July 27, 2026. It passed the Lok Sabha on July 29 and the Rajya Sabha on July 30, and received presidential assent on July 31, 2026.

The Act covers examinations conducted by the Union Public Service Commission, Staff Selection Commission, Railway Recruitment Boards, Institute of Banking Personnel Selection, National Testing Agency, Central Government ministries and attached offices, and other authorities notified by the Central Government.

For individuals using unfair means, imprisonment increases from 3–5 to 5–10 years, and the maximum fine increase from ₹10 lakh to ₹50 lakh. For service providers, the maximum fine rises from ₹1 crore to ₹5 crore and debarment expands from up to four years to eight years. Proportionate examination costs shall also be recovered.

Directors, senior managers or persons in charge who consent to or connive in an offence face 5–10 years’ imprisonment and a ₹5 crore fine, compared with 3–10 years of imprisonment and a fine of ₹1 crore earlier. Organised crime attracts 7–10 years’ imprisonment and a minimum ₹10 crore fine, compared with 5–10 years of imprisonment and a fine of a minimum ₹1 crore fine under the 2024 Act.

The amendment introduces a two-month investigation period, counted from the date of recording information for police investigations, referral for central agencies, and the date of the notification constituting a Special Task Force (STF).

Every state and Union Territory must designate one or more Courts of Session as Special Fast-Track Courts in consultation with Chief Justice of the relevant High Court. Trials must be completed within three months of filing the charge sheet, or within three months of transfer in pending cases. State governments and UT administrations must appoint Special Public Prosecutors under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023.
Appeals lie before a two-judge High Court bench, normally within 30 days, with an absolute 90-day limit. Appeals should be disposed of, as far as possible, within three months of admission.

CETA facilitates temporary movement of business visitors, intra-corporate transferees, contractual service suppliers, independent professionals and investors.

DCC prevents dual social-security contributions for eligible temporarily posted or detached workers.
Ordinary overseas employees generally contribute in their country of employment.
It concerns contribution liability and does not automatically grant host-country pensions or other contributory benefits.

India’s Academic Freedom Index (AFI) score declined from 0.16 in 2024 to 0.14 in the latest assessment.
The report documented 382 attacks arising from 321 verified incidents involving higher-education communities across 59 countries and territories between 1 July 2025 and 30 June 2026.
Free to Think is an annual publication of the Scholars at Risk Academic Freedom Monitoring Project, examining threats to academic freedom, institutional autonomy and higher-education communities.
The Index measures actual levels of academic freedom across 179 countries and territories.
It is jointly implemented by Germany’s Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU) and the V-Dem Institute, using assessments from 2,357 country experts.

The Index evaluates: 1. Freedom to research and teach. 2. Freedom of academic exchange and dissemination. 3. Institutional autonomy. 4. Campus integrity. 5. Freedom of academic and cultural expression.

the United States, Denmark and Greenland signed a new Arctic Defense Agreement at the United Nations Headquarters in New York, strengthening military cooperation and security in the Arctic and North Atlantic.

The agreement, signed by US President Donald Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenland’s Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen, expands US military access while recognising Denmark’s sovereignty and Greenland’s right to self-determination.
The agreement amends the 1951 Defense Agreement concerning Greenland and will enter into force after the necessary parliamentary procedures in Denmark and Greenland are completed.
The original US–Denmark Defense Agreement was signed on 27 April 1951 under the framework of the North Atlantic Treaty.
It was subsequently supplemented by the 1991 Memorandum of Understanding and the 2004 Igaliku Agreement.
The agreement permits the expansion and modernisation of US military activities at Pituffik Space Base, formerly known as Thule Air Base, in north-western Greenland.
The facility supports ballistic missile early warning, missile defence, satellite tracking and space surveillance.
The agreement also refers to the proposed US Golden Dome missile-defence system.
The agreement promotes greater North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) involvement in Arctic military planning, exercises, intelligence gathering, surveillance and interoperability.
It generally prohibits non-NATO countries from establishing military installations or maintaining a persistent military presence in Greenland without the parties’ agreement.

a powerful 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck western Colombia, with its epicentre near San José del Palmar in Chocó Department, at a depth of approximately 103 km.

Colombia lies in north-western South America, bordering both the Pacific Ocean and Caribbean Sea.
Its seismic activity is influenced by the interaction of the Nazca, South American and Caribbean tectonic plates.
Along Colombia’s Pacific margin, the oceanic Nazca Plate subducts beneath the continental South American Plate.
This convergence generates tectonic stress, causing earthquakes, crustal deformation and volcanic activity.
Colombia is part of the Circum-Pacific Belt, extending approximately 40,000 km around the Pacific Ocean.
This tectonically active region experiences frequent earthquakes and volcanic eruptions due to convergent plate boundaries and subduction zones.
The subduction of the Nazca Plate beneath the South American Plate produces compression, crustal folding and uplift, contributing to the formation of the Andes Mountains.
Fluids released from the descending plate also promote magma formation and volcanism.

The Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (PMJDY) completed 12 years on
expanding access to formal banking and financial services among underserved and economically disadvantaged sections.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi launched PMJDY on 28 August 2014 as India’s National Mission for Financial Inclusion.
India’s Financial Inclusion Index increased from 53.9 in 2021 to 67 in March 2025.
In January 2015, Guinness World Records recognised 18,096,130 bank accounts opened in a single week (from August 23-29, 2014) under the Department of Financial Services campaign.
Eligible account holders receive a RuPay debit card, accepted at ATMs and most Point-of-Sale terminals. Banks had issued 41.29 crore cards by 19 August 2026, promoting digital payments.
Accident insurance cover increased from ₹1 lakh to ₹2 lakh for new accounts opened after August 28, 2018.
An overdraft of up to ₹10,000 is available to one eligible account holder per household, ordinarily after six months of satisfactory account operation and subject to prescribed conditions.

Accounts increased approximately fourfold from 14.72 crore in 2015 to 59.09 crore by 19 August 2026. Rural and semi-urban areas held 45.95 crore accounts, or 77.8%, while urban and metropolitan areas held 13.14 crore.
Women held 32.92 crore accounts, or approximately 55.7% of the total, as of 19 August 2026, reflecting greater gender equality in formal financial access.
Deposits increased approximately twentyfold from ₹15,670 crore in March 2015 to ₹3,16,514 crore in August 2026. Average deposits reached ₹5,356 per account on 19 August 2026.

The Government of India has approved a proposal by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) for field trials of ₹10 and ₹20 polymer banknotes.

The RBI proposed one billion notes of each denomination, totalling 200 crore notes with a face value of approximately ₹3,000 crore. The Government informed Parliament of the approval in 2026, when procurement remained at an initial stage. Regular issuance may be considered only after successful trials.

The RBI submitted the proposal under Sections 24 and 25 of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, following its Central Board’s recommendation. Section 24 covers the banknote denominations whereas Section 25 covers design, form and materials.
Bharatiya Reserve Bank Note Mudran Private Limited (BRBNMPL),
an RBI subsidiary, initiated polymer-substrate procurement.
Polymer banknotes use a non-fibrous, non-porous plastic film. Existing Indian paper banknotes use long cotton fibres from cotton comber and cotton linter.
Polymer notes will circulate alongside existing ₹10 and ₹20 paper notes, which will remain legal tender. Trials will assess cleanliness, security, handling and suitability for India’s cash economy.

The Bankers’ Books Evidence Act, 2026 came into force on October 1, 2026. The Act replaces the Bankers’ Books Evidence Act, 1891 with a technology-neutral framework recognising physical, electronic and digital banking records as evidence. The definition of bankers’ books includes records at off site, virtual, cloud, backup and disaster recovery locations. Banks and bankers also include post office savings bank and money order offices.
The Lok Sabha passed the Bill on 5 August 2026 and the Rajya Sabha on 10 August. Presidential assent followed on 13 August 2026.

The first schedule applies to copies of books maintained in written or physical form. The second schedule applies to copies of books maintained electronically, digitally or through other data storage mechanism.
Certificates must confirm accuracy and be authenticated manually, digitally or electronically by an authorised bank officer.
Digital records are admissible if created and stored in the ordinary course of banking through regularly used, properly functioning systems.
Certified copies are prima facie, not conclusive, evidence where original entries are legally admissible.
The Central Government may extend coverage by notification. NBFCs, payment aggregators and fintech firms are covered only if notified or under another law.

Introduced in the Lok Sabha on 3 August 2026, the Indian Statistical Institute Bill, 2026 seeks to replace the 1959 Act (came into force on April 1, 1960). It would convert ISI into a statutory body corporate while retaining its status as an institution of national importance.
Body-corporate status would provide clearer legal authority and institutional continuity. ISI would remain under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation.
The President of India would be the Visitor, empowered to order reviews or inquiries and issue binding directions. The Visitor would nominate the Board’s Chairperson on the Centre’s recommendation.
Admissions would follow transparent, merit-based criteria without discrimination.

An 11-member Board would replace the 33-member Council as the principal policy-making and executive body, accountable to the Centre. It would comprise the Chairperson, government representatives, four external experts and four ISI representatives.
The Board would approve budgets, plans, fees and regulations, reorganise academic units and award degrees on the Academic Council’s recommendation.
would include Centre-Directors, all full-time Professors, selected faculty and the Dean of Academic Affairs.
The Director would be the Chief Executive Officer, managing daily administration and implementing institutional decisions.
ISI may receive government grants after parliamentary appropriation, earn revenue, accept donations and maintain funds.

The Viksit Bharat – Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act, 2025, or VB-G RAM G Act, is India’s statutory framework for rural wage employment and village development. It came into force across rural India on July 1, 2026, repealing the
Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, 2005 (MGNREGA).

Rural Development Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan released over ₹25,000 crore as the first installment, called the Mother Sanction, to support timely wage payments. A total ₹7.5 lakh crore (as on July, 2026) will be invested in 2.86 lakh Panchayats over the next five years. Wage rates have increased by around 10 percent on average.

The Act guarantees wage employment, strengthens village economies and promotes sustainable livelihoods. It links employment with productive public assets, transparency, convergence, climate resilience and local economic development, following “Rozgar Bhi, Samman Bhi”, or employment with dignity.
Key Features of the VB-G RAM G Act
The Act increases the employment guarantee from
100 to 125 days per financial year for rural households
whose adult members volunteer for unskilled manual work.
The notified minimum wage floor for 2026–27 is ₹300 per day.
Wages should be paid weekly or within fifteen days of work and muster-roll closure measures delayed compensation.
Delays attract compensation of 0.05 percent of unpaid wages per day beyond the sixteenth day after closure.
Existing e-KYC-verified job cards remain valid until Gramin Rozgar Guarantee Cards are issued. Workers may register at Gram Panchayats, and pending e-KYC cannot justify denial of employment.
Work may be demanded orally, through Form-6 or digitally.

Failure to provide employment within the prescribed timeframe entitles workers to unemployment allowance of at least one-fourth of the notified wage for the first thirty days of the financial year and one-half for the remaining period.
Water security; Rural infrastructure; Livelihood infrastructure; Climate resilience.

The Act operates as a Centrally Sponsored Scheme, with a 90:10 funding ratio for Northeastern and Himalayan States (like Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh and Jammu & Kashmir); and it is 60: 40 for other States and UTs with legislatures.

UTs without legislatures receive full Central funding. Central allocations follow objective, rule-based parameters. States bear expenditure beyond normative allocations and must distribute funds transparently according to local needs.

For FY 2026–27, the Central share is ₹95,692.31 crore, described as the largest Budget Estimate allocation for a rural employment programme. Including the estimated State share, total outlay is expected to exceed ₹1.51 lakh crore.

the National Statistics Office under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) released India’s first Trial Index of Services Production for April 2026.

The ISP is India’s first high-frequency macroeconomic indicator measuring short-term changes in the volume of formal services output relative to a base year. It fills a statistical gap because the Index of Industrial Production does not capture changes in services activity.
As of July 24, 2026, the trial covered 19 sub-sectors representing about 60% of the services economy, without a single overall ISP.
Fourteen sub-sectors recorded double-digit year-on-year growth in April 2026 compared with April 2025.
Accommodation and food services led year-on-year growth at 37.2%, followed by retail trade (30.8%), administrative and support services (28.7%), real estate (27.7%) and telecommunications (22.8%).
During 2025–26, annual growth was 35.6% in accommodation and food services, 30.5% in retail trade, 25.1% in repair services, 23.6% in wholesale trade and 22.6% in road transport.
The base year is 2024–25, aligning the ISP with revised economic indicators and broadly with the new Consumer Price Index series, whose reference year is 2024.

In late June 2026, the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) supervised India’s first Satellite-Based Landing System (SLS) approach by a commercial jet using the indigenous GAGAN system. An IndiGo Airbus A321 conducted the demonstration using satellite-derived guidance instead of relying on a conventional Instrument Landing System (ILS).
GAGAN (GPS Aided GEO Augmented Navigation) is India’s indigenous Satellite-Based Augmentation System developed by the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) and the Airports Authority of India.

It enhances GPS accuracy and provides integrity information for safer aircraft navigation. Certified to international standards, GAGAN supports satellite-based landing and serves sectors beyond aviation.

GAGAN operates through an integrated network of ground stations, communication systems, and geostationary satellites. These elements monitor GPS signals in real-time, calculate corrections, and broadcast enhanced navigation information to aircraft.

A team of scientists from the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) on
shared a report of the findings of the ‘Hop’ experiment conducted by the Vikram Lander of Chandrayaan-3 and the Chandra’s Surface Thermophysical Experiment (ChaSTE) on the Moon.
A new study conducted during the final phase of the Chandrayaan-3 missions when the Vikram lander performed a successful hop experiment, has offered fresh insights into the Moon surface.

During the final phase of its mission, Chandrayaan-3’s Vikram lander reignited its engines to perform a controlled “hop” experiment (primarily to test ascent capabilities for future sample-return missions) and landed nearby, nearly 50 cm away from its initial position.
ChaSTE (Chandra’s Surface Thermophysical Experiment), a lunar thermometer was re-penetrated into the lunar regolith (soil) at the new location.

By analysing the ChaSTE data following this historic “hop” monoeuvre by the Vikram lander, scientists have discovered that the post-hop location at the Moon’s southern polar region possesses a complex, layered soil structure that was significantly altered by the lander’s brief flight.
Key findings from the study have emerged, which include:

analysis revealed a distinct two-layer structure within the top 6.5 cm of the post-hop site which means that the top few centimetres of the Moon’s surface aren’t just a uniform pile of dust; they are made of distinct layers with different properties,
the soil’s cohesion and density were found to increase significantly with depth which means that the Moon’s soil at the surface becomes more packed and sticky as we go deeper and
the data highlighted a “shadowing effect” where local craters and depressions caused temperatures to plunge faster than global models predicted.
The engine firing blew away the top 3 cm of regolith, exposing and slightly compacting the material underneath.

Artemis II was not a Moon-landing mission; it was a

meant to prove that NASA’s Space Launch System, Orion spacecraft, ground systems, recovery teams and mission procedures can safely carry humans beyond low Earth orbit and bring them back. NASA describes it as the first crewed Artemis flight and a key step toward long-term human return to the Moon and future crewed missions to Mars.

Artemis II lifted off from the Kennedy Space Center on April 1, 2026, sending the first humans to the Moon since 1972. (Note: The Apollo 17 mission in 1972 sent humans to land on the Moon, whereas Artemis II sent humans toward the Moon.)
During the mission, the crew completed a lunar flyby, returning humans to the Moon’s vicinity for the first time in 53 years after the final Apollo Mission to the Moon.

The Artemis II Orion heat shield is the critical thermal protection system on the base of Orion Spacecraft. Orion heat shield protect the Capsule and Astronauts from searing temperatures and Extreme friction during high speed atmospheric re-entry.
During the flight, the astronauts tested Orion’s life-support, communications, control, navigation and manual operation systems in a deep-space environment.
The mission also tested how well astronauts could live and work inside Orion during a lunar-return flight.
This is important because Artemis is not only about reaching the Moon; it is about building the systems needed for repeated journeys, lunar surface work, and eventually Mars missions.
The Orion Spacecraft used in Artemis II was named Integrity by the crew.
Orion’s Heat Shield and Re-entry Lesson
One of the most important engineering lessons came from Orion’s heat shield. During Artemis I, NASA found unexpected cracking and shedding of heat-shield material.

NASA later explained that heat and gases had accumulated inside the Avcoat material, creating internal pressure and uneven shedding during re-entry, although the spacecraft would still have kept a crew safe.
For Artemis II, NASA closely monitored re-entry and the thermal protection system.

The spacecraft returned at extremely high lunar-return speed, and NASA’s initial inspection found that the heat shield performed as expected and that heat-shield char loss was significantly reduced compared with Artemis I.
This result is important for astronaut safety in future Moon-landing missions.
Artemis III is now listed by NASA as a 2027 low-Earth orbit demonstration, mission to test one or both commerical landers from SpaceX and Blue Origin.

India’s heavy-lift launcher LVM3 (Launch Vehicle Mark-3) has been increasingly used for high-value national missions as well as international commercial launches. In the LVM3M6 mission, ISRO/NSIL launched the BlueBird Block-2 communications satellite of AST SpaceMobile (USA) and successfully placed it into the intended orbit.
The Indian Space Research Organisation’s (ISRO) Launch Vehicle Mark-3 (LVM3) on December 24, 2025 and successfully placed the BlueBird Block-2 satellite in its intended low Earth orbit.

ISRO accomplished two milestones with this mission as it was able to deploy the largest commercial communications satellite in low Earth orbit and also the BlueBird Block-2 satellite became the heaviest payload (6,100 kg.) to be launched by LVM3 from Indian soil.
LVM3-M6 mission was the 104th launch from Sriharikota and also the ninth successful mission of the LVM-3 launch vehicle and the third dedicated commercial mission demonstrating its 100% reliability.
AST SpaceMobile (AST & Science, LLC) is building the space-based cellular broadband network, which is accessible directly by smartphones and designed for both commercial and government applications.
AST SpaceMobile has launched five satellites — BlueBird 1-5 in September 2024, which enable non-continuous internet coverage across the US and other select countries.
The BlueBird Block-2 satellite features a 223 m2 phased array, making it the largest commercial communication satellite ever deployed into low Earth orbit.
The BlueBird Block-2 mission is part of the global Low Earth Orbit constellation to provide direct-to-mobile connectivity through a satellite.
This constellation would enable 4G and 5G voice and video calls, texts, streaming and data for anyone at any time, ISRO said.
The BlueBird Block-2 spacecraft launched heaviest payload into Low Earth Orbit in the history of the LVM3 rocket on December 24, 2025.

articles.title: JAMA Blood Group in Humans

runs: The International Society of Blood Transfusion (ISBT) has recognised JAMA as the 49th human blood group system, numbered ISBT 049. The discovery followed a joint investigation by researchers in the United Kingdom and Israel into unusual blood samples from a woman and her brother. ISBT ratified the system at its Kuala Lumpur Congress in 2026 and announced it on
The finding adds to the understanding of rare blood characteristics and their possible importance in transfusion medicine.
Blood plays a vital role in the human body, carrying oxygen and essential nutrients to cells. For years, A, B, AB and O have been the blood groups most familiar to people.
Now, scientists have identified a new blood group system called JAMA, taking the total number of recognised blood group systems to 49.
The International Society of Blood Transfusion (ISBT) has officially recognised JAMA as the 49th blood group system.
The discovery came from a joint investigation by researchers from the UK and Israel. It began when scientists examined the blood of an Israeli woman and her brother.
The woman was found to have an antibody that reacted with the red blood cells of most people.
However, the same reaction did not occur with her own red blood cells or those of her brother.
This unusual result caught researchers’ attention because the antibody did not correspond to any previously identified blood group antigen.
JAMA should not be viewed as another category alongside A, B, AB and O. Instead, it is a separate blood group system involving a specific antigen.
This antigen is found on the red blood cells of most people. In the woman and her brother, however, it was absent.
Their blood also contained a corresponding antibody, helping scientists identify the unusual blood group characteristics.

runs: Bengaluru-based Astrobase Space Technologies unveiled EVEREST, which it describes as India’s first fully integrated, privately developed Full-Flow Staged Combustion (FFSC) rocket engine. As of
full-scale integrated hot-fire testing remained pending, so reported performance figures were company-stated design targets.

FFSC engines route fuel and oxidiser through separate pre-burners before the main combustion chamber. Gases produced drive turbines connected to pumps and then enter the chamber, ensuring that propellants contribute to thrust instead of being released into the atmosphere.

Unlike conventional engines, which use only part of the propellants to drive turbopumps, FFSC engines improve turbopump and propulsion efficiency. They support precise throttle control and reusable launch systems. LOX-methane propellants provide cleaner combustion, which can simplify refurbishment and support faster turnaround. However, the cycle is complex to design, develop and execute.

EVEREST is presented as India’s first LOX-methane high-thrust engine and the fourth commercial FFSC development globally, after SpaceX, Stoke Space and LandSpace. It could support reusable launches carrying up to 30 tonnes to low Earth orbit and provide a medium-lift platform for commercial and strategic missions. Ethanol is a renewable alcohol fuel. India’s Ethanol Blended Petrol (EBP) Programme mixes domestic ethanol with petrol to reduce crude-oil dependence, support farmers and rural industry, and lower road transport’s environmental impact.

E5, E10 and E20 contain about 5%, 10% and 20% ethanol by volume. E20 combines anhydrous ethanol with 80% petrol. Since November 2023, the Ethanol Supply Year (ESY) runs from 1 November to 31 October. India first achieved 20% blending in 2025; the November 2025 – August 2026 average was 20%. Public-sector outlets normally supply E20; premium grades XP100, poWer100 and Speed100 remain ethanol-free. From 1 April 2026, notified blended petrol requires a minimum Research Octane Number of 95.

Pilots began in 2001, and the EBP Programme launched in 2003 in nine States and four Union Territories. The 2018 National Policy on Biofuels targeted E20 by 2030; the 2022 amendment advanced it to ESY 2025–26. E10 was achieved in June 2022, and phased E20 rollout began on 6 February 2023.

Capacity grew from 421 crore litres in 2014 to about 2,000 crore litres in 2026. Procurement was about 38 crore litres in ESY 2013–14 and was projected to exceed 1,200 crore litres in ESY 2025–26. The 10 July 2026 update reported cumulative gains since ESY 2014–15: foreign-exchange savings exceeding ₹1.97 lakh crore, nearly 316 lakh tonnes of crude substitution, around 952 lakh tonnes of CO2 reduction and farmer payments exceeding ₹1.66 lakh crore.

E10 predominates in the United States; E85 contains about 51–83% ethanol and is intended for flex-fuel vehicles. Brazil mandated E30 from 1 August 2025. Brazil temporarily introduced E32 in ordinary and additivated petrol from August 1, 2026 for 180 days with one possible equal extension. Japan targets direct E10 by FY 2030 and E20 by FY 2040. India helped launch the Global Biofuels Alliance in September 2023 to promote sustainable biofuels, standards and best practices.

runs: According to the Bihar Economic Survey, 2025–26, Bihar’s Gross State Domestic Product (GSDP) at constant (2011–12) prices grew by 8.6 percent in 2024–25 (Q.E.), and at current prices by 13.1 percent, reaching ₹5,31,372 crore and ₹9,91,997 crore respectively.
In the last three years, Bihar’s economic growth rate, both at constant and current prices, has been higher than the Gross Domestic Product growth rate of India.
At current prices, Bihar’s GSDP growth rates were 17.9 percent in 2022–23 and 14.9 percent in 2023– 24, compared to 14.0 percent and 12.0 percent respectively for the country.

The quick estimates for 2024–25 show that Bihar’s GSDP growth rate at current prices is estimated at 13.1 percent compared to 9.8 percent for India. At constant (2011–12) prices, Bihar’s growth rate is estimated at 8.6 percent, which is higher than India’s 6.5 percent. These figures place Bihar among the fastest-growing states in the country.
For 2024–25, quick estimates show that the Gross State Value Added (GSVA) of the secondary sector grew by 11.1 percent at constant (2011–12) prices and 15.5 percent at current prices.

In 2024–25, the tertiary sector grew by 8.9 percent at constant prices and 13.5 percent at current prices, while the primary sector recorded growth of 4.1 percent at constant prices and 9.6 percent at current prices.

Between 2020–21 and 2024–25, the share of the secondary sector in GSVA increased significantly from 21.1 percent to 26.8 percent at constant (2011– 12) prices, mainly due to growth in construction and manufacturing.

In contrast, the share of the primary sector declined from 21.9 percent to 18.3 percent, and the share of the tertiary sector also declined from 57.0 percent to 54.8 percent, indicating increasing diversification in the state’s economic activities.
Per capita GSDP at current prices increased from ₹46,412 in 2020–21 to ₹76,490 in 2024–25, indicating a consistent upward trend.
At constant (2011–12) prices, per capita GSDP increased from ₹30,159 in 2020–21 to ₹40,973 in 2024–25.
Within Bihar, Patna district recorded the highest Gross District Domestic Product (GDDP), followed by Begusarai and Munger districts.
At current prices, per capita GDDP was ₹2,41,220 for Patna, ₹1,05,600 for Begusarai, and ₹93,921 for Munger.

Bihar’s fiscal development path reflects disciplined financial management, as the state government’s total expenditure increased from ₹1.66 lakh crore in 2020–21 to ₹2.82 lakh crore in 2024–25. The state government maintained fiscal prudence through moderate borrowing and effective debt servicing while consistently prioritising developmental expenditure in sectors such as education, health, energy, transport, irrigation, and agriculture.
This structural change reflects the government’s focus on long-term investment, infrastructure development, and asset creation.

Revenue receipts of the state government increased from ₹1.28 lakh crore in 2020–21 to ₹2.18 lakh crore in 2024–25, with tax revenue as the main source. The share of tax revenue increased from 70 percent to 84 percent, while the share of non-tax revenue declined from 5 percent to 2 percent and the share of grants-in-aid declined from 25 percent to 14 percent.

The structure of revenue expenditure remained largely stable over the last five years, with social services having the highest share at 46 percent. The share of economic services increased slightly from 21 percent in 2020-21 to 22 percent in 2024-25, while the share of general services declined slightly from 33 percent in 2020-21 to 32 percent in 2024- 25.
This distribution reflects the government’s commitment to both welfare expansion and strengthening productive sectors.

The share of plan expenditure in total expenditure increased from 38.3 percent in 2020–21 to 39.9 percent in 2024–25, while the share of establishment and committed expenditure declined from 61.7 percent to 60.1 percent.
This trend indicates a gradual shift towards welfare-oriented activities and policy-driven development priorities.

Developmental expenditure remained around two-thirds of the total budget, reaching 67.4 percent in 2024–25. It increased from ₹1,12,122 crore in 2020– 21 to ₹1,89,892 crore in 2024–25, indicating a stronger focus on development and welfare expenditure.

Receipts from the central government increased from ₹91,625 crore in 2020–21 to ₹1,59,298 crore in 2024–25, mainly due to transfers from the divisible tax pool, which increased from ₹59,861 crore in 2020-21 to ₹1,29,435 crore in 2024-25.
In 2024–25, grants-in-aid from the central government amounted to ₹29,863 crore.
The state’s own revenue increased from ₹36,543 crore in 2020–21 to ₹59,360 crore in 2024–25, with tax revenue as the major contributor.
As of 31 March 2025, the outstanding debt of the state government was ₹3,74,134 crore, which was 37.7 percent of the GSDP.

At the end of 2024–25, 84.6 percent of the total outstanding debt consisted of public debt. Out of total public debt, 83.8 percent came from internal borrowings, while 16.2 percent came from loans and advances from the central government.
Market loans and loans from financial institutions are the main components of internal debt.

According to provisional estimates released by the Directorate of Economics and Statistics for 2023– 24, agriculture, forestry, and fisheries together accounted for 23.1 percent of GSVA. Within this, crop production contributed 11.5 percent and livestock contributed 8.1 percent.

In 2023–24, rice, wheat, and maize together contributed 99.9 percent of total cereal production in Bihar. In 2024–25, rice accounted for 40.7 percent, wheat for 32.1 percent, and maize for 27.1 percent of total cereal production.
Between 2023–24 and 2024–25, production of rice increased by 4.3 percent, wheat by 7.1 percent, and maize by 12.6 percent.

Bihar is among the leading fruit and vegetable producing states in the country and is a major producer of litchi, makhana, and mushrooms. In 2023–24, total horticulture production in the state was estimated at about 230 lakh tonnes, which is higher than 206 lakh tonnes in 2019–20, with a major share coming from fruits and vegetables.
Between 2023–24 and 2024–25, milk production increased by 4.2 percent, egg production by 10.0 percent, and fish production by 9.9 percent.
The share of electricity consumption in agriculture increased significantly from 5.3 percent in 2020–21 to 14.9 percent in 2024–25.

In 2024–25, the number of Kisan Credit Card holders increased by 16.3 percent compared to 2023–24, while total credit disbursed increased by 32.8 percent from ₹7,080.07 crore in 2023–24 to ₹9,399.24 crore in 2024–25.

Total expenditure on irrigation in 2024–25 was ₹2,729.83 crore, of which 74.3 percent was capital expenditure. Between 2023–24 and 2024–25, total irrigation expenditure increased by 63.1 percent. This increase in public expenditure is reflected in the extensive expansion of major, medium, and minor irrigation projects.

Bihar’s secondary sector has experienced fluctuations over the past five years. After a sharp decline in 2020–21 due to the pandemic, it recovered in 2021– 22 and recorded rapid growth in 2022–23, mainly driven by mining, utilities, and construction.
In 2024–25, 37.8 lakh tourists visited 28 eco-tourism sites, which is 24.0 percent higher than the previous year. Total outlay for eco-tourism and park development in 2024–25 was ₹100.00 crore.

Over the past 19 years, expenditure on social services has increased rapidly, rising fivefold in the first decade and 15-fold between 2005–06 and 2024–25. Expenditure on health and education increased by 14.8 times and 13.2 times respectively.
Life expectancy at birth (LEB) in Bihar during 2019–2023 was 68.9 years for males and 69.7 years for females.
It is also notable that between 2017 and 2023, the infant mortality rate (IMR) declined by 12 points from 35 to 23.

Significant progress has been made in reducing maternal mortality Ratio (MMR), which declined from 312 deaths per lakh live births in 2004–2006 by 208 points to 104 in 2021–2023. Under the Janani Suraksha Yojana, institutional deliveries increased from 15.77 lakh in 2020–21 to 16.17 lakh in 2024–25 (an increase of 2.54 percent).

In 2024–25, total enrolment at the elementary level school is 159.22 lakh, including 80.87 lakh boys and 78.35 lakh girls. Total enrolment was 27.54 lakh at the secondary level and 20.33 lakh at the higher secondary level.
Environment, Climate Change and Disaster Management

Between 2011–12 and 2024–25, Bihar’s forestry and logging sector achieved a compound annual growth rate of 10.4 percent at current prices. The total value increased from ₹4,187 crore to ₹15,139 crore during this period.
By 2024–25, this sector accounted for 7.0 percent of GSVA in agriculture and 2.0 percent of the state’s total GSVA.
Since 2011, Bihar’s ecological footprint has expanded significantly. The total area under forest and tree cover increased by 689 sq km from 9,214 sq km to 9,903 sq km by 2023.

The total forest cover increased from 6,845 sq km to 7,532 sq km during this period. Notably, the area under very dense forests (VDF) increased significantly from 231 sq km to 387 sq km, indicating successful conservation within protected areas.

Bihar’s commissioned power capacity is 11,764 MW, with the major share coming from thermal power (7,743 MW). Solar energy is the largest renewable source with a contribution of 1,922 MW, followed by hydropower at 1,356 MW and wind energy at 699 MW.
In 2024–25, the total budget allocation for the Urban Development and Housing Department was ₹5,274.9 crore and total expenditure was ₹3,613.8 crore, with a utilisation rate of 68.5 percent.

The credit-to-GSDP ratio in Bihar increased steadily over the last five years from 30.9 percent in 2020–21 to 37.9 percent in 2024–25, indicating increased availability of credit in the state’s economy.
The percentage of non-performing assets (NPAs) in banks in Bihar declined significantly over the last five years from 11.8 percent in 2020–21 to 7.6 percent in 2024–25.

The Unique Identification Authority of India (UIDAI) launched the Aadhaar mascot, a new resident-facing communication companion to simplify public understanding of Aadhaar services on January 8, 2026.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi unveiled the name of the building complex Seva Teerth on February 13, 2026.
He also formally inaugurated Seva Teerth (Prime Minister’s Office etc.) and Kartavya Bhavan-1 & 2 (accomodate key ministries).
Tripura Gramin Bank (TGB) has achieved a historic milestone by becoming the first Regional Rural Bank (RRB) in India to introduce a solar-energy-based mobile ATM van (TGB on wheels) in January 2026.
Assam-based Numaligarh Refinery Limited (NRL) was accorded ‘Navratna’ status (27th CPSE) on December 2, 2025.

The National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) has signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Reliance Jio to introduce a telecom-based safety alert system across the National Highways network in December 2025.
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) granted in-principle approval to Fino Payments Bank for transitioning into a small finance bank in December 2025.

According to a press release on October 15, 2026, the Asian Development Bank (ADB) and the Government of Japan signed financing agreements with AM Green Ammonia (India) Private Limited to develop one of the world’s largest renewable energy-based ammonia plants in India.

It marks the first investment under the Action for Creating Energy Security for Long-term Resilience (ACCEL) and includes a $100 million loan from the Leading Asia’s Private Infrastructure Fund 2, financed by the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) and administered by ADB.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank Group (WBG) Managements released the Bangkok Blueprint, a high-level framework developed in coordination with the Bank of Thailand on October 14, 2026.
It aims to help countries prevent, detect, and address the growing threat of cyber-enabled fraud in digital financial services.
China's Northwestern Polytechnical University (NPU), in collaboration with Xi'an Tianhe Maritime Technologies, set a new Guinness World Record by
conducting coordinated formation navigation of 116 Autonomous Underwater Vehicles (AUVs) simultaneously.

According to the university's official press release dated September 24, 2026, the achievement was certified by Guinness World Records in the category of ‘Most Autonomous Underwater Vehicles Operating Simultaneously’.
The record attempt was conducted on August 29, 2026, under the supervision of official Guinness World Records adjudicators and experts.
On August 15, 2026, SpaceX launched two Falcon 9 rockets only 38 minutes apart, establishing a new record for the shortest interval between two orbital launches conducted by a single launch provider.
The first Falcon 9 lifted off at 9:12 p.m. EDT from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida while the second Falcon 9 was launched at 9:50 p.m. EDT from Vandenberg Space Force Base, California.
SpaceX’s previous record was 65 minutes, established on August 31, 2024 through two consecutive Starlink launches from Florida and California.
The International Cricket Council (ICC) Board has approved the admission of Mauritius as the 111th Member of the ICC on July 15, 2026.

On July 3, 2026, the Asian Development Bank (ADB) has approved a $230 million loan to modernize and expand Chennai’s water supply and sanitation infrastructure, benefiting 4.5 million residents in the Greater Chennai area.
The project will construct over 170 kilometers of water supply pipes and sewer pipes, upgrade seven water pumping stations and 38 sewer pumping stations.
Chennai will become the first Indian city to implement a comprehensive ring-main solution.
The World Health Organization (WHO) has added the first molecular diagnostic test for Bundibugyo virus (BDBV) to its Emergency Use Listing (EUL) on July 2, 2026.
The test detects the virus by identifying its genetic material in blood samples, helping confirm infection rapidly and accurately.
The National Institute of Food Technology Entrepreneurship and Management, Kundli (NIFTEM-K), has entered into a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Massey University, New Zealand on July 2, 2026.
Saudi Arabia joined the International Big Cat Alliance (IBCA) as its new member on May 22, 2026.
Ghana joined the International Big Cat Alliance as its new member on October 7, 2026.
Bangaladesh joined IBCA as its new member in June, 2026.
As of now, 29 countries have joined IBCA as members.

In light of the reported outbreaks of Ebola Disease in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Uganda, the World Health Organization (WHO) on May 17, 2026, under the International Health Regulations, 2005, determined it to be a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC).

The Ministry of Education, Government of India handed over the Letter of Approval (LoA) to the University of Liverpool, United Kingdom, to establish its branch campus in Bengaluru, Karnataka on June 4, 2026.
Microsoft unveiled Majorana 2, its next-generation topological quantum chip developed with the help of Microsoft Discovery’s agentic AI in June 2026.
Majorana 2’s new features include a new materials stack enabling a 1,000-fold improvement in reliability over the prior generation of qubits.

The World Health Organization (WHO), on April 24, 2026, has announced a significant step forward in the fight against malaria with the prequalification of the first treatment developed specifically for newborns and young infants weighing between two and five kilograms.
The World Health Organization (WHO) has verified Chile for eliminating leprosy disease in March 2026.
It has become the first country in the Americas – and the second globally – to be officially verified as having eliminated leprosy disease.
The United States Government formally exited from the World Health Organization on January 22, 2026.
The World Health Organization (WHO) has validated Fiji for eliminating trachoma as a public health problem on October 20, 2025.

The Asian Development Bank (ADB) projects India’s gross domestic product growth to ease to 6.9% in fiscal year 2026 (FY2026, ending 31 March 2027)—from 7.6% in FY2025, according to the Asian Development Outlook (ADO) April 2026, released on April 10, 2026.

The World Bank Group and the Government of Sri Lanka, on April 2, 2026, launched a new five-year Country Partnership Framework (CPF) to support Sri Lanka’s continued recovery, help achieve its 7% medium-term economic growth target.
Singapore Changi Airport has been named the Airport of the Year 2026 at the 2026 World Airport Awards ceremony held in London on March 18, 2026.
The airport has reclaimed the top position for the 13th time.

Bahrain, Colombia, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Latvia and Liberia have begun two-year terms as non-permanent members of the United Nations Security Council (UNSC), replacing Algeria, Guyana, the Republic of Korea, Sierra Leone and Slovenia on January 1, 2026.
They join the other five non-permanent members – Denmark, Greece, Pakistan, Panama and Somalia – who will serve through the end of 2026.
Etihad Airways was named the world’s safest full-service airline for 2026, according to a report from AirlineRatings.com, released in January 2026.
It became the first Gulf carrier to top the list.

India has been re-elected to the IMO (International Maritime Organization) Council for the 2026-27 biennium in Category B, comprising 10 countries with the largest interest in international seaborne trade. on November 28, 2025.
